content: To establish confidence in the clinical safety of the product, it is essential to assess tolerance in patients participating in phase 2 trials. A thorough review of clinical safety parameters must be conducted, which includes both a comprehensive literature review and adherence to the provisions outlined in the trial protocol. If the population in phase 3 trials has broader inclusion criteria compared to the more restricted populations in earlier trials, the favorable safety profile observed in prior studies may not necessarily apply to the broader population. Additionally, the larger sample size in phase 3 trials increases the likelihood of detecting rare adverse events, making it critical to re-evaluate safety parameters during this phase. Preliminary efficacy data from phase 2 trials should be carefully considered. Informed consent must be obtained, participant selection must be equitable, and the risks and benefits must be weighed to ensure they are favorable for potential participants. Furthermore, the experimental design must be robust and scientifically sound. Specific concerns related to clinical trials involving herbal products include: The potential for product adulteration and whether it has been documented. Interactions between herbal remedies and other substances, which are often poorly understood. Limited data on reproductive and organ toxicity. Incomplete prior dose-finding studies. These uncertainties must be transparently communicated to all stakeholders, particularly during the informed consent process. Where feasible, the community from which the herbal medicine originates should be consulted during the research process, and the results and benefits of the research should be shared with this community. As with other types of research, the involvement of well-trained and ethical investigators is the best assurance of patient safety. Skilled clinicians should be selected as investigators to ensure the prompt recognition and appropriate management of any adverse events or exacerbations of pre-existing conditions. Herbal substances refer to materials derived from plants through processes such as extraction or mechanical manipulation. Herbal products are the administered forms of these substances, also known as herbal remedies, herbal medicines, herbal drugs, or botanical drugs. The active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) is the chemical constituent responsible for the therapeutic effect of the herbal substance or product. Chemistry-manufacturing-control (CMC) encompasses the chemical and manufacturing processes, as well as the controls applied to these processes, used to produce the herbal substance and product. Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) are a set of standards ensuring that CMC procedures are performed to the highest possible quality. Feedback and suggestions on all aspects of this operational guidance are welcomed for consideration in future revisions.
